subject: A4A06D2046A34125BE345C7E50F25812
introduction: “By corruption of the text is meant … the interpretation of God’s holy Book in accordance with their idle imaginings and vain desires.” The guide begins with that redefinition and tests it against history: prophecies taken literally, so that the Promised One did not match; tales of marvels grown round a verse; tradition and the learned standing between a people and its Book; then, within the Bábí and Bahá’í story itself, charges of plagiarism, of alteration and of forged verses. Scripture has always carried this warning inside it. The tempter quotes a psalm; Peter says the unstable wrest Paul’s letters; the Qur’an speaks of those who distort the Scripture with their tongues and of the ass carrying books; John’s crowds reject Jesus on a literal point about Galilee. But the other side is heard too. Aquinas founds every sense on the literal; the Talmud answers a heavenly voice with “It is not in heaven”; most Muslims read “Seal of the Prophets” plainly; Paul curses any other gospel; Jeremiah accuses real scribes of real falsification; Spinoza and Mill ask what any authority over meaning must answer for.
questions: The Qur’an speaks both of distorting scripture “with their tongues” and of writing it “with their hands”. Why does the guide insist that corruption is chiefly of meaning, and what follows from that?

The first readings condemn altering the “evident meaning”; later ones condemn taking prophecy literally. With Aquinas and the rabbis’ rule of the plain sense in view, how can one tell which words are evident and which symbolic?
John’s crowds had good scriptural reasons for expecting the Messiah from Bethlehem. What, in the readings, should have told them their reading was mistaken?
“It is not in heaven”, say the rabbis; the Bereans search the scriptures daily. When is a learned tradition a veil, and when is it the way a community reads faithfully?
Paul tells the Galatians to accept no other gospel; the Bayán tells its readers not to let it veil them from the One to come. How can a book prepare its readers to go beyond it?
The guide closes with casting the Book “behind their backs” and with Paul’s “we see through a glass, darkly”. What habits of reading would keep a reader from both faults?

outside.why: The reading quotes this verse. The Qur’an charges a party of an earlier people with hearing the word of God and changing it knowingly, “after they had understood it”; the reading takes that to mean changing its sense.

Corruption is “interpretation … in accordance with their idle imaginings”. The Qur’an’s own description is of the tongue, not the pen: they distort the Scripture with their tongues, that ye may think it is from the Scripture.
A Christian letter says the same of Paul’s epistles: there are things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do the other scriptures.

Another verse does speak of hands: woe unto those who write the Scripture with their hands and say, “This is from God”. Many Muslim scholars read it of the text itself. What turns on whether corruption is of the wording or of the meaning?
A man quotes only “that which is useful to your own purpose”. Antonio in The Merchant of Venice: the devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
The pattern has a famous instance. On the pinnacle of the temple the tempter quotes a psalm accurately, and is answered with another verse.
“Great error may result from the misinterpretation of a single word.” Jesus speaks of a law in which not one jot or tittle is negligible.
Blake to a fellow reader: “Both read the Bible day and night, / But thou read’st black where I read white.”
If the Gospel in people’s hands were not from God, grace would have ceased. The Gospel’s own claim for its words is that they shall not pass away.

Spinoza opened the modern study of the Bible by arguing that the Pentateuch was not written by Moses but long after. Must the reading’s confidence that the Gospel has not been lost deny what such study finds?
Whoever “altereth its evident meaning” has perverted the Word. Deuteronomy’s rule for the text: ye shall not add unto the word, neither shall ye diminish ought from it.
The rabbis have a rule for the “evident meaning”: a verse does not depart from its plain sense, whatever else is drawn from it.
“Corrupt not the holy … Word of God.” Proverbs: every word of God is pure; add thou not unto his words, lest thou be found a liar.

People “cling to their own desires, imagining themselves to be turning toward the truth”. Bacon classified such self-deception as idols that beset the mind, from the tribe, the cave, the market-place and the theatre.
They “have taken a word from the Book and interpreted it” to their wish. Isaiah mocks a religion reduced to fragments: precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little.

“They seek to prove what they believe through the verses while denying Him Who revealed them.” Jesus says the same to scholars of scripture: ye search the scriptures, and they testify of me, and ye will not come to me.
Some lift phrases from prayers and attribute them to themselves. Jeremiah: I am against the prophets that steal my words every one from his neighbour.
Traditions report altered words and letters in the Qur’an. Its own verse answers: We reveal the Reminder, and We verily are its Guardian.
New verses differ from old “if you look at their outward meanings and neglect their inner significances”. Paul: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.

Aquinas admits several senses in scripture but insists that all are founded on the literal, from which alone argument can be drawn. If inner significance may override the outward, what restrains the interpreter the first stretch warned against?

Conditions were taken literally, and so “This Promised One is not that Promised One”. In John the crowd reasons the same way: shall Christ come out of Galilee? Hath not the scripture said, out of Bethlehem?
They expected a sovereign conqueror. Another group in John has another literal condition: when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is; but we know this man.
Even disciples held the expectation. On the road to Emmaus: we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.
Sun, moon and stars in the Gospel are not to be read outwardly. Origen asked in the third century what intelligent person could think the first days of Genesis had evening and morning without a sun.
The text in question: the sun darkened, the moon not giving her light, the stars falling from heaven.
Signs were set which, taken outwardly, gave an excuse. Elijah was to come first; Jesus says that Elias is come already, and they knew him not.
Maimonides read the prophets’ signs as figures: that the wolf shall dwell with the lamb is a parable of peace among peoples, and nature keeps its course.
The verse behind the tale: “The hour drew nigh and the moon was rent in twain.” The reading rejects the story built on it as astronomically childish.

Has superstition about miracles gathered round the founders’ lives? Emerson told the divinity students of Harvard that the word Miracle, as pronounced by the churches, gives a false impression; it is Monster.
There were many Gospels and manuscripts, too many to alter in concert. Luke begins by acknowledging that many had taken in hand to set forth the story.

“Through the lapse of time human ideas have crept in.” The translator of Sirach admits another quiet change: things uttered in Hebrew have not the same force in another tongue. How much of what a reader meets is the translator?
Tradition “veiled Him so completely”. Jesus’s own charge: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.

The Talmud tells a story against the reading’s view of it: a heavenly voice sides with one rabbi, and the others answer “It is not in heaven”; interpretation belongs to the community of the learned. Is tradition a veil over the text, or the only way a text is ever read?
Each age’s divines objected to its Messenger. Stephen to the council: which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?
The reading cites these demands: a spring gushing from the earth, a house of gold, a book sent down. The Qur’an records them and answers: am I aught save a mortal messenger?
Demands for a sign of one’s own choosing. Abraham in the parable: if they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.
Two great turbans debate idle questions as divine knowledge. Pope: a little learning is a dang’rous thing.
“Each day they would claim some new understanding.” The pastoral letter has a phrase for it: ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
The sign expected was withered trees turning green. Jesus to those asking a sign from heaven: ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
A belief held for twelve centuries, on pain of death, proved unfounded. Milton: a man may be a heretic in the truth, if he believes only because his pastor says so.

The reading names “the Seal of the Prophets” as an explicit text that was nevertheless overturned in men’s understanding. To most Muslims the plain sense of this verse is finality. Who decides when a plain sense is a misreading?
They “interpreted this word according to their own imaginings”. Nicodemus, a master of Israel, hears “born again” and asks how a man can enter his mother’s womb a second time.
They have “veiled themselves behind the veils of allusions”. Paul: when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart.
“We cause them to hear … but they hearken not.” Isaiah’s commission: hear ye indeed, but understand not; see ye indeed, but perceive not.
“They follow the ignorant and call them learned ones.” If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
Reminded by the Book, “yet they perceive not”. Jesus gives it as the reason for parables: seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
The learned who thought themselves “oceans of knowledge” failed. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
“Woe unto every learned one whom knowledge hath withheld.” Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in, and them that were entering ye hindered.
The Bereans are called noble because they searched the scriptures daily to see whether the new teaching was so. Learning there serves recognition. What makes the same learning a veil?
They “ask of the drop concerning the ocean”. The voice from the whirlwind asks Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid.
“Do they not see the rising of the Sun of inner meanings?” The light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
Many saw the rain of mercy fall and gained nothing. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
The Bayán was revealed “that ye should not” be veiled by it from its fulfilment. Had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.
“Let not the Bayan veil you from Him.” Paul says of the law that it was a schoolmaster to bring us to Christ; after faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.
The Báb answers a questioner: I am a servant who has believed in God. Muhammad is told to say the like: am I aught save a mortal messenger?
New verses echo old ones, and are called borrowed. The Preacher holds that there is no new thing under the sun. When scripture resembles scripture, is that theft, or what one would expect?
He is said to have “plagiarized the verses of the Point”. The officers sent to seize Jesus report on what they heard, not on its sources: never man spake like this man.
“The sightless ones” explain the revelation away. Nazareth does the same with what it cannot account for: from whence hath this man these things? Is not this the carpenter?
Paul’s judgment on his own people and his former self: they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
One denier says the Revelation “hath appeared too soon”. Every expectation carries a timetable. Whose calendar was it?
“Are ye more powerful than God?” The risen Jesus to disciples who ask about the timetable: it is not for you to know the times or the seasons.
They read the Báb’s words and misunderstand. Philip’s question to the Ethiopian reading Isaiah: understandest thou what thou readest? How can I, except some man should guide me?
“Names have prevented most”: successor, guardian, mirror. Juliet: what’s in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
Titles become parties. Corinth: I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas. Is Christ divided?
They measure a station “by their own vain imaginings”. My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
Some identify the Promised One with the Báb himself. The priests ask John the Baptist whether he is Elias or that prophet; he says, I am not.

“They read what We revealed aforetime and reject that which is greater.” The scribe instructed unto the kingdom brings out of his treasure things new and old. Is fidelity to the earlier book always a refusal of the later?
“You neither wrote it nor obeyed.” Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.

Paul warns his converts that though an angel from heaven preach any other gospel, let him be accursed. The Bábís who hesitated could have quoted him. How does a community that is told to hold fast also stay ready?
One “has denied the Book of God and has intended to eliminate it”. King Jehoiakim cuts Jeremiah’s roll leaf by leaf and burns it.
An attempt “to obliterate the Bayan”. Milton: who destroys a good book, kills reason itself.
“None has been, nor ever shall be, able to alter the Bayan.” The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
“They say the Bayan has been altered.” Jeremiah himself makes that charge against the scribes of his day: the pen of the scribes is in vain. The accusation is not always a calumny; how is it tested?
“They cling to the Book while turning away from the Lord.” The Pharisees to the man born blind: thou art his disciple; but we are Moses’ disciples.

The old saying, that the Book has been corrupted, returns. The Qur’an on those who received a messenger confirming what they had: they flung the Scripture of God behind their backs as if they knew not.
Verses stolen, erased, counterfeited. Paul’s churches already had to be warned of a letter “as from us”.
“They added some fabricated ones.” The last page of the Bible threatens whoever adds to the words of the book.
He “falsified the Words of the Blessed Beauty”. Second Peter expects it from within: there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies.
The remedy named is documentary: obtain the declaration and read it. Paul’s remedy was his signature, the token in every epistle.
A body “will gather together all the Sacred Writings” and pronounce. The apostles and elders came together to consider a disputed matter, and wrote their finding.

Dissent from the finding “would be severely dealt with”. Mill held that to silence a contrary opinion is to assume one’s own infallibility. The reading locates authority in a body it trusts to be guided; what does Mill’s objection still ask of those who obey it?
Rumour said He had abolished fasting, prayer and the law. The same was said of Jesus, who answered: think not that I am come to destroy the law; I am come to fulfil.
Those who knew not a letter of the Cause spoke as their desires bade. James: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak.
The learned “issued the decree for the death of the Lord”. The time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
“They interpreted but did not attain.” The Qur’an distinguishes clear verses from allegorical, and says those with doubt in their hearts pursue the allegorical, seeking dissension.
“For six thousand years misunderstandings have kept humanity divided.” Montaigne: there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things.
“Imitations have crept into religions.” Emerson: the idioms of Jesus’s language and the figures of his rhetoric have usurped the place of his truth; churches are built on his tropes.
The reading cites this saying: put up again thy sword into his place, for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
“Consider the Christian wars.” Gibbon chronicled what was done under the banner of the cross by those who had that sentence in their scriptures.
The reading quotes the cry over the molten calf. Corruption there is not of a text at all but of worship, within weeks of Sinai.
“The deaf man and the trumpet, the mirror in the hand of the blind.” Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine.
“One who has taste perceives the flavor.” The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit; they are spiritually discerned.
The psalm’s invitation supposes the same faculty: O taste and see that the Lord is good.
No worship avails the one who wavers. He that is not with me is against me.

Micah asks what the Lord requires and answers: to do justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly with thy God. The reading makes recognition the condition of worship. What would each say of the other’s test?
The reading’s phrase is scriptural: Israel’s confession says the fathers cast thy law behind their backs.
They “cast the Book of God behind their backs”. The psalm to the wicked: what hast thou to do to declare my statutes, seeing thou castest my words behind thee?
The Qur’an has the Messenger’s own complaint: O my Lord! mine own folk make this Qur’an of no account.
Those “who play with God’s verses”. The Qur’an’s image for bearers of a scripture they do not apply: the ass carrying books.
The guide’s arc ends in humility. Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part. If every reader sees darkly, what protects the readers of this guide from the errors it lists?

nehemiah-cast-thy-law-behind-their-backs.text: Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against thee, and cast thy law behind their backs, and slew thy prophets which testified against them to turn them to thee

proverbs-add-thou-not.text: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar

matthew-tradition-none-effect.text: Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition

psalm-cast-my-words-behind-thee.text: What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Seeing thou hatest instruction, and casteth my words behind thee

quran-used-to-listen-then-change-it.text: Have ye any hope that they will be true to you when a party of them used to listen to the word of Allah, then used to change it, after they had understood it, knowingly?

quran-distort-the-scripture-with-their-t.text: And lo! there is a party of them who distort the Scripture with their tongues, that ye may think that what they say is from the Scripture, when it is not from the Scripture. And they say: It is from Allah, when it is not from Allah; and they speak a lie concerning Allah knowingly.
